speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a short statement respecting the letter from Mr. Khrushchev which was handed to me on Saturday by the Soviet ambassador. This letter was in reply to my letter to Mr. Khrushchev of May 9. The contents of the letter received have been carefully studied in the hope that it might contain promise of progress toward a settlement of some at least of the differences between our country, and in particular the question of disarmament.
The letter, unfortunately, reveals the continuing refusal of Mr. Khrushchev to understand the intentions of the Canadian government in supporting the proposal made recently in the United Nations security council for a system of control in the Arctic
regions. This proposal was an honest endeavour on the part of Canada and its allies to work out measures of control over military activities on this important frontier which would give security to all countries participating, including the Soviet union. We have not had, nor do we have, any intention, as suggested in the letter to us, of imposing a system of inspection on the Russians. We are, however, seeking to work out in collaboration with them and our other Arctic neighbours a system which will satisfy the needs of all and remove the fears, from whichever side they may arise, of air attack launched without warning. For our part we are continuing to study the possibilities of such a system of control in the hope that the Soviet union will come to recognize that this system would play an essential part in any effective scheme of security and disarmament.
Mr. Khrushchev's letter is, however, not entirely negative. It does indicate willingness on the part of the Soviet union to go along with proposals recently made by President Eisenhower for an immediate study of methods for controlling the suspension of nuclear tests. I have made clear our anxiety that progress be made in this important aspect of disarmament, and welcome this promising sign. If this fruitful project is to be carried out, good will and a spirit of forbearance are required on all sides. For this reason, therefore, I will refrain from taking issue with Mr. Khrushchev over the misrepresentations and allegations in his letter and emphasize rather the more hopeful aspect of his message.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion gives me an opportunity to bring to the attention of the house, ultimately in the form of a motion, a matter of very great importance to the house and the country; namely the failure -or if not failure certainly the unwarranted delay on the part of the government-to call a federal-provincial conference to discuss unemployment and other urgent problems of common concern to both federal and provincial authorities, and in particular to give an assurance that the government would maintain or improve the principle of equalization of direct tax revenues of the provinces embodied in the present law.
This problem of fiscal relations between federal and provincial governments is inevitable in any federal system. Its origin
Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations lies in the uneven division of wealth and resources and income among the different parts of the federation, coupled with the necessity, on grounds of national unity, of the central government doing everything possible to lessen these disparities. Wealth in a country like Canada tends to accumulate to a greater extent in some areas and provinces than in others, and those others naturally feel deprived of adequate means for growth, welfare and economic security.
The problem also arises out of the fact that national policies, which are essential to unify and strengthen the country as a whole, may have an uneven impact on various sections and provinces. If the central government did not try, by financial contributions, to correct these inequities, national unity certainly would suffer. And this particular problem is always more acute in a time of depression or recession or pause, as we learned in the thirties.
That is another reason why discussion and action are desirable at this time. The motion I will move will not only give the government an opportunity to do something about this important problem at this time, when something should be done, but will give new members from Quebec, Ontario and the other provinces a chance to speak on this problem; the problem whether the federal government should share taxes with the provinces and if so, on what basis and by what formula and, above all, how much should the wealthier provinces, which have larger sources of provincial income than some of the other provinces, claim from the shared taxes.
The Liberal party and Liberal governments have always accepted the obligation of action in this field of federal-provincial relations, and our record in this matter is clear and good. I suggest that in this case the vision of the future or difficulties of the present should not be permitted to obscure and distort the record of the immediate past. In this case, as in other cases, it is not difficult to answer the question, "What did you do", which hon. gentlemen opposite like to throw at us as we discuss this and other problems, so perhaps I should go into the record for a few moments.
In 1935, in the midst of the depression some provinces in our federation were or. the verge of bankruptcy and the federal system was breaking down under the pressures of depression and unemployment. Hon. members will recall that in 1935 the Rowell-Sirois commission was set up to examine the problem of fiscal relations in the light of that situation, and in due course that commission presented a plan for grants in aid from the central government which, as these
728	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations grants were to be made on the basis of need, did embody the principle of equalization.
This plan was not accepted by the provinces. Nevertheless, during the years steady progress was made by Liberal governments in Ottawa toward their objective of an agreement for the single collection and equitable division of the three important direct taxes which, under our constitution, are shared between the federal and provincial governments. As hon. members know, those three taxes are the personal income tax, corporation income tax and succession duties.
It seems obvious that these taxes, if they are to be collected by the federal government, must be shared between the two levels of government in a way to permit both levels to perform their functions and carry out their obligations to their people. It is very often complained, and it has been complained more than once by the Minister of Finance, that the federal share of these and other tax revenues has gone up in recent years to the detriment of the provinces. Of course the federal share has gone up but so have federal expenditures for defence, expenditures arising out of the war such as veterans aid and all that kind of thing. Federal expenses have also gone up because of direct contributions made by the federal government to the provinces, direct transfer payments for education, health and other purposes.
Whereas it may be charged, as it sometimes
is,	that 70 per cent or even more of the taxpayer's dollar now goes to the federal government, if allowances are made for these payments made by the federal government to the provincial governments that figure must be greatly reduced. If that calculation is made, and perhaps the minister has made
it,	it will perhaps be found that having regard to these transfer payments the proportion of the taxpayer's dollar now taken by the federal government is not higher than it was in 1939.
It might be argued, of course, that it would be better and would avoid complications and difficulties if the provinces collected their own taxes in these three fields at their own rates, as they do in other fields of taxation. That, however, would be fair only if the provinces were close enough together in wealth and resources to permit of approximately the same amounts per capita from the same levels of taxation in these three fields.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Would the hon.
gentleman permit a question? Did I understand correctly that he was challenging me to prove that the federal share of the tax

dollar was greater in 1939 than in 1956? Would he elaborate on that? What are his figures?

No; I was suggesting to my
hon. friend that if in making this calculation at the present time he makes allowance for transfer payments to the provinces from the federal government and for the growth in expenditures for national defence, for instance, which affect all the Canadian people, he may find that the percentage of the taxpayer's dollar collected by the federal government in 1958 is not greater than that collected in 1939. I said if that calculation were made allowance must be made for transfer payments and these other defence and war expenditures.
I had just said that it might be argued that it would be better if the provinces collected their own taxes at their own rates in these three fields of taxation. I also said that would only be fair if the provinces had approximately the same wealth and resources so they would get approximately the same amounts from the same levels of taxation. But as we know that, of course, is not the case. A provincial income tax at a rate which would bring in large revenue in the province of Ontario would bring in very little indeed in the province of Prince Edward Island. Therefore, as we see it, the best plan is central collection at a single rate with a division of the total which, through equalization provisions, would permit every provincial government to provide adequate services to its own people.
Equalization in this sense means that where per capita revenue from the shared fields of taxation falls below an agreed amount, however calculated, federal contributions will make up the difference. I suggest that the putting forward, establishment and acceptance of this equalization principle is one of the most important domestic achievements of Liberal governments in recent years. Indeed, I would go further and say that its acceptance in some suitable form is important, and perhaps that may be an understatement, to the preservation of national unity in our federal system, and it can and must be applied by agreement and with a minimum of federal interference with and no infringement of provincial rights.
There is no centralism in this, Mr. Speaker, but there is a desire to strengthen the position of all the provinces in the federation and thus strengthen national unity.
On January 14, 1955, a new plan was put forward by the Liberal government of that day as a substitute for previous tax-rental agreements. This plan laid down a definite equalization formula based on the per capita

average receipts of the two wealthiest provinces from the three shared taxes. In putting forward this plan at that time the prime minister of that day, Mr. St. Laurent, had this to say:
The present government has no intention of abandoning the objective of the tax-rental agreement which is to make it financially possible for all provinces, whatever their tax base, to perform their constitutional functions themselves and to provide a reasonable Canadian level of provincial services without an abnormal burden of taxation.
He added:
That is the foundation of the policy of the federal government.
This remains the foundation of the policy of our party in this field. The tax-sharing plan that was put forward at that time was not, of course, perfect, but it certainly seemed better at that time to all concerned than anything else that had been proposed. For the first time all the provinces which accepted the arrangement would receive approximately equal shares of these three direct taxes paid by Canadians. We on this side of the house, Mr. Speaker, are proud of the achievement in developing and putting forward that proposal. It embodied progress made in the solution of this problem over the years.
In order to indicate what progress had been made, may I just suggest to the house that at the end of the war, in 1945, the provinces received in tax rentals-the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) mentioned this the other evening-about $92 million. But in the last fiscal year, 12 years later, under the tax-sharing and equalization plan they received $631 million. Our last year in office as a Liberal government saw the provinces receiving $114 million more than under the tax-sharing arrangement of the preceding year, or an increase for that year of 20 per cent. Of course, Mr. Speaker, all the provinces at that time wanted still more; that was understandable. They were not satisfied; that was natural. I shall have a little more to say about this in a moment, but that is the inevitable problem a federal government must face in trying to share revenues with provincial governments.
The Minister of Finance of that time, Mr. Harris, put this problem in a statement to the House of Commons after the last conference in 1956, as follows:
While there seems to have been a general acceptance of the principle of equalization-
That was at the dominion-provincial conference.
_there is, I realize, some conflict of views on
the manner in which it has been applied. Some provinces with very substantial taxable capacity feel that their responsibilities are such that they should be accorded still more room in these tax fields. Other provinces, where taxable capacity is
Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations below the average, press for still larger equalization or fiscal need grants. The federal government is squeezed between these conflicting views.
I suspect that the Minister of Finance is beginning to feel that squeeze now. Wealthier provinces like Ontario, whose premier at that time thought that province did not get enough and that the plan proposed was too generous to certain other provinces, wanted more. Less wealthy provinces, like the Atlantic provinces and Saskatchewan, which felt that fiscal grants should supplement even equalization payments when the need justified it, also wanted more. It was the federal government's responsibility then, as it is the federal government's responsibility at any time, to strike a balance between these claims, and that balance was established by the late government by a formula which we know as 10-9-50, 10 per cent of the personal income tax, 9 per cent of the corporation tax and 50 per cent of the succession duties to be turned over to the provinces, with equalization payments based on the per capita average receipts of the two wealthiest provinces.
This formula, or even the very principle of a formula of sharing, was not accepted by the province of Quebec. So far as Ontario was concerned only the personal income tax formula was accepted, and this under protest as being too low. The premier of Ontario, Mr. Frost, in more than one appearance with the Prime Minister during the election campaign of 1957, demanded more money and a higher formula. He indicated that the government of Ontario would insist on what is known as the 15-15-50 formula which would bring Ontario, if it were applied, more than $100 million over the formula which was then in effect. I believe it is fair to say that the people of Ontario were led to believe at that time that Ontario would get that formula only under a Conservative government, and that they would get it under a Conservative government.
Well, what did the Conservative government do? As we know, it increased the percentage of personal income tax to 13 per cent for one year only. It was estimated, and perhaps the estimate may not turn out to be too accurate in view of falling revenues, that this would bring in about $62 million, of which Ontario would get more than one-third or $22 million. This change was made, but it was not made at any conference with the provinces. There was no conference at which this change was agreed upon, but the change was made by the federal government and notification of it was sent to the provinces by telegram. There were even some mathematical errors in the computations first made.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, it was a queer way of doing business by a government the

-simply said-
In respect of these earlier arrangements.
-"These are the terms." No opportunity was given for amendment or for amelioration of any terms. The recipe for a division of taxation was as final as the laws of the Medes and Persians . . .
There was no opportunity for negotiation; there was simply the attitude of a feudal lord bringing into being a modern feudalism and laying down the law to the vassals.
Well, if that was the attitude taken by the present Prime Minister to arrangements then made, which had been discussed at a provincial conference, I wonder what he would have said if he had been on this side of the house in regard to the procedure adopted to bring the plan into effect last January.
Now, leaving procedure aside for the moment, let us look at these various formulae to see what they would cost the national treasury and also what they would give the wealthiest province, Ontario, if they were applied. The Liberal formula of 10-950, as I think I have already stated, would have brought in $631 million for the provinces, of which Ontario would get $216 million. The Conservative formula for one year only at 13-9-50 will cost the federal treasury $683 million, and of that amount the province of Ontario will get $238 million or $22 million more. The formula put forward by Premier Frost as the only one that would be acceptable to the province of Ontario of 15-15-50, without any provision for equalization, would cost the federal treasury, if my figures are correct, $760 million, of which the province of Ontario would get $332 million. If the equalization principle were included in that formula and calculated on the basis which Mr. Frost said would be the only tolerable one-and he was opposed to equalization in principle-that would cost the federal treasury $846 million; and if it were calculated on the basis of the two highest provinces it would cost the federal treasury almost $1 billion.
Was the premier of Ontario satisfied with the decision which was made last autumn, and which gave him $22 million more? To illustrate his feelings in that regard when this announcement was made and his reaction to it, perhaps I might read a short statement by the Liberal financial critic in the Ontario
IMr. Pearson.]

legislature at that time, in February, 1958, when this matter was under discussion, and the reply of the premier of Ontario to this statement later during the course of his own budget debate. In February of this year Mr. Wintermeyer in the Ontario house had this to say:
He-
That is Mr. Frost.
-personally did more to defeat the Liberal government in Ontario than any other man alive, and he did it because the people of Ontario believed that, when he said he needed $100 million and that they were holding it back unlawfully and inequitably from him, they believed him, and they supported him and voted a government out of power.
A new government took over-
Continued Mr. Wintermeyer.
-on June 10 and it seems wholly inconsistent that he should come back to this legislature at the expiration of one year-
Referring to Mr. Frost.
-and say: "Gentlemen, I have made an arrangement. I do not know exactly what this arrangement is, but it is an instalment for interim payment on what 1 still say that government owes." That is not what he said a year ago. A year ago his words were; "We will make them disgorge, if necessary, that $100 millions. It is ours. It is owing to us."
In the year 1957 not one red penny of that $100 million was paid to us. In the year 1958-59 there has been a promise of some. I ask, how much? What faith has Mr. Frost in the promise of the Right. Hon. Premier of Canada?
In the budget debate of that time, February 26, 1958, Mr. Frost replied to that statement as follows:
Ontario has made it plain that the province's share of the main direct tax fields should not be less than 15 per cent of the federal personal income tax, 15 percentage points of corporation income and 50 per cent of federal succession duty collections in each province ... I have said Ontario needs $100 million more in direct taxation.
We know what that means in terms of dollars and cents. Last Thursday night, I think it was, in this house the hon. member for Essex East addressed this question to the Prime Minister as reported at page 665 of Hansard:
Does he now suggest that this government has fully met the demands made by the province of Ontario when the premier of that province has said he wants an additional $78 million from the government of which my hon. friend is the head?
The reply given by the Prime Minister was this:
The provinces will naturally place the very best claim they possibly can place before their people and the country as a whole.
I think this house has the right to know, and I think the people of Ontario would like to know, whether the Ontario government's demand for 15-15-50, with what that

implies in contributions from the federal treasury, is to be accepted by this government as its policy for aid to that province and the others.
This situation or this dilemma, if you like, into which the government has fallen because of its statements may have something to do with the failure of the government to call a conference at this time to settle the matter. Certainly during the 1957 election campaign- and this is on the record already in this house-the Prime Minister said he would summon a conference immediately to deal with this problem. We know what happened. "Immediately" was November. The conference lasted two days and did not deal in any effectual way whatever with this problem, and did not deal with unemployment in any effectual way either.
As a matter of fact, as my friend the hon. member for Essex East pointed out the other night, in 1955 when there was much less unemployment in this country than there was last November we who were on the other side of the house at that time were pilloried day after day by members of the opposition for not calling a provincial conference immediately to deal with the unemployment problem, which was not half as serious as it was last November and as it is today. Yet no conference with the provinces has been called yet to deal with that problem.
We know what the figures are. As of April 17 the dominion bureau of statistics figures show 516,000 unemployed still in this country as compared with 306,000 a year ago. On April 30 claims for unemployment insurance fell-there was a drop, I admit-but they still show 722,000 as opposed to 373,000 at the same date last year. If that does not justify the calling of a conference to deal with this problem, what could?
Furthermore, has this problem of taxsharing and equalization been dealt with? Not in any way whatever. On November 26 the conference to which I refer met for a couple of days and then adjourned to meet early in this year. Did it meet? Has it met? The answer is no. It could not meet before the election, according to the Prime Minister, because members of parliament were spending too much time asking questions.
May I say that we are still asking questions. Surely that is not the reason the conference has not met in April or in May or in June of this year. Or is there some other hidden reason, arising out of the expenditure promises made by the government and their relation to the worsening position of the federal treasury? If that is not true perhaps the Minister of Finance will enlighten us.
2, 1958
Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations
Certainly we have had no enlightenment with regard to this matter up to the present time. The Minister of Finance has not yet, after all these months, given us the accounting that he promised for last autumn. All we know is that in January of this year he estimated a surplus for the year that is past. We know, because it is common knowledge, that revenues have declined while expenditures are increasing, though not as fast as promises to spend are increasing. There is surely a problem here of reconciliation which will tax even the ingenuity, agility and financial acrobatics of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: And the late hours of the Minister of Finance.

Perhaps that may have a bearing on the delay in holding a provincial conference at this time. Mr. Frost wants more from a federal treasury which is not, to say the least, flourishing, and he is not to be held off by $22 million. There is the indecision of the government over the equalization principle; whether to accept it and, if it accepts it, how to apply it. A conference with the provinces might not be too happy a meeting at this particular time.
There is another question about which I would like to say a few words, and that is with respect to the special grants to the Atlantic provinces. It must be recognized, indeed it is recognized by all members, that the lower average income of the Atlantic provinces makes the position very difficult in respect to providing, even with equalization payments, the kind of services all Canadians should have. I admit at once, as indeed we admitted last autumn in this house, that the special grants that were given were helpful, but we criticized them and we still criticize them because they are not based on any formula which would make possible their general application to all provinces. In other words they are not based on any; principle; they are a hand-out.
Surely a better way than that could be found to give that kind of assistance, valuable as this assistance has been. In order to make my point I would like to quote from one who certainly could not be accused of having any political leanings or political prejudices in this matter. I have in my hand the speech of the president of the Atlantic provinces economic council, made in Montreal, I believe, on March 7 or at least in that week, and he is reported in the press as follows:
What is needed first, however, is a changed attitude in all provinces. At present people think of national development in terms of power stations and pipe lines in the west, the seaway here in central Canada, and the opening of the north.

Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations
But once attention is turned east of Quebec to the Atlantic area, people think of aid, assistance, subsidies, subventions and the like. Useful and welcome as they are, they are not national development; they are more like economic tranquilizers which are dangerous when taken alone and in too large quantities and which can lead to overdependence. Let us stop thinking of the Atlantic provinces in terms of aid alone, and regard them as a region ready for, and worthy of, some of the same developmental projects that all of us now support in the rest of Canada.
The Halifax Chronicle Herald, on January 28, had something to say on this subject in an editorial from which I quote as follows:
The Atlantic provinces are appreciative of these grants but would prefer to have the same policy applied to them that applies to the other taxsharing payments-variations from year to year with a fixed floor.
We on this side of the house feel that they should be adjustable and should be flexible, and that the formula for calculating them should apply to all provinces. That would make it a part of national policy. In other words, in Atlantic provinces grants and all other grants, the principle of equalization with a fixed floor should be applied and a new formula adopted for that purpose. This reference to a fixed floor is just another way of saying that grants of this kind and formulae which are adopted and changed subsequently should always include provisions for stabilization.
Let us look for a moment at this question of stabilization, what it means and what the attitude, in so far as we have been able to determine it, of the government is with respect to it. It presents another horn of the dilemma on which the government finds itself. In the 1956 act, passed by a Liberal government, the tax agreements provision, as my hon. friend knows so well, provided that each province should be guaranteed a payment for the fiscal year 1958-59-that is, the subsequent fiscal year-of not less than 95 per cent of what was received the previous year.
Surely the importance of that provision will be obvious to every member of this house, especially at a time of falling revenues. I believe the Liberal government at that time showed commendable foresight in putting that provision into the agreement. Today revenues will not have to fall very far to make the Conservative formula of 13-9-50 return even less than our formula of 10-9-50, because no stabilization provisions were included in the new act of last January. Under that formula, because of falling revenues and because of the absence of this stabilization provision, they may receive no increase at all and indeed only 95 per cent of what they got last year which, under the


stabilization provision of the Liberal government in the year before they were bound to get in any event.
Perhaps even more important than this question of stabilization is the government's attitude toward equalization, especially in view of the fact that demands of the provincial governments, particularly Ontario, are being made for a new formula which would provide more income for them. I have already mentioned the difficulty over the policy insisted upon by Mr. Frost, the premier of Ontario, and that policy makes the question of equalization more important than ever, especially for the less wealthy provinces. If Ontario is going to get more-and Ontario certainly expects more-are all to get more? The Prime Minister during the election campaign appeared to accept Mr. Frost's rejection of equalization, and to accept on the other hand the historical position of his party which was opposed to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, rubbish.

If my hon. friend thinks that is rubbish let him look up the record in Hansard and his own vote at the time with respect to the tax agreements provision, and the attitude of his party with respect to this whole matter of equalization.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was not a vote on the principle of stabilization or on the principle of equalization. It was a vote to condemn the insufficiency of your payments.

We in this party have challenged the government and the Prime Minister on more than one occasion, and perhaps my hon. friend will clear away this difficulty right now when he gets up to speak in this debate. We have challenged them more than once to say specifically and definitely that no province, Ontario or any other province, would be given preferred treatment in any way and that any increase in payments would be spread equitably; in short, that the principle of equalization would be maintained on a proper basis. We over here have taken our stand that there should be no special deals which are not applicable to all who qualify for extra help. A year ago our questions were not answered, and again during the election campaign they remained unanswered. Furthermore, in the last session the same questions were not answered, and we were told that a provincial conference would be called immediately which would answer all these questions. However, they were not answered and since that time we have been told nothing, with one qualification to which I will come in a few moments.
The premier of Manitoba has asked in letters for the same assurances for which we

asked regarding equalization, and he did not get them. The matter was pressed, as I think my hon. friend will agree, at the provincial conference last November, without result. Then during the recent election campaign in Winnipeg on February 12 the Prime Minister did promise to retain the equalization principle in future dominion-provincial tax agreements. I suggest that in that statement he reversed the policy of his party which had been oposed to equalization payments in principle-
He never did.
-and had voted against tax agreements which contain that principle.
You are building a straw man to knock down; that is what you are doing.
If my hon. friend wants to speak on this matter let him refer to Hansard and read the record of his party, and let him put that record on Hansard now.
Let him ask the Solicitor General too.

And the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer). Let him say something about the matter. Conservative members will have lots of opportunity to clarify their views and their government's attitude during the course of this debate. Indeed, that is one of the reasons this motion is being moved. However, while the Prime Minister was in Winnipeg during the election campaign in February last he accepted the principle of equalization. But he has said nothing since that time, as he said nothing at that time about the nature and scope of the equalization action he supports.
Not only is the principle important, but the application of that principle is even more important. On what basis are equalization payments going to be made? As far as this party are concerned we are pledged to equalization on the basis of the per capita yield of the three taxes in the wealthiest province. We made that proposal during the election campaign, and we stand by that policy in this House of Commons at this time as being the basis which is fairest, especially to the less wealthy provinces.
Surely it is just as important to establish the right basis for equalization as it is to support the principle itself. If we take another basis, for instance the national average, which has been favoured by some people, or if we take the basis of the top four provinces, we will get a different result and a result not nearly so satisfactory, especially to the less wealthy provinces. If, for instance, we were to take the basis of the national average, equalization payments would amount only to
Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations $64 million, while on the basis we are advocating they would amount to $163 million. Liberal policy with regard to both the principle and the basis of the application of equalization has been declared, and on that we stand. I hope the government in the course of this debate will make its own position equally definite and equally clear. Indeed the fact that we do not know what is the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite is, I suggest, a main reason why a conference should be called after that policy has been made clear, perhaps in this house during this debate.
It surely seems perfectly obvious to all reasonable people that a provincial-federal conference should be called at this time. Joint action on unemployment is required now, and action is also required to prepare for a situation which next year may necessitate even more effective and far-reaching measures. We hope the situation will not require such action, but surely it would be wise to prepare for such a situation now, and to prepare for it jointly with the provinces. If it was essential to have this kind of meeting in 1955, when a meeting did not turn out to be necessary because the unemployment problem was not so serious, surely it is far more essential to have one now when the unemployment problem is at least twice as serious as it was then.
A conference is also required, Mr. Speaker, because of this question of fiscal relations which is now being dealt with on an ad hoc, piecemeal, one-year basis. It should be settled now according to some principle which would give some form of security to the provinces for the future, particularly in respect to equalization; how this would be brought about and upon what basis. No longer should there be doubt and delay on these important matters. The government has a duty to take action now, action which it has so far refused to take.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin):
That all the words after the word "that" be deleted and the following be substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that the government has failed to call a federal-provincial conference to discuss unemployment and other urgent problems of common concern to federal and provincial authorities; and that the government has failed to give assurance that it would maintain or improve the principle of equalization of direct tax revenues of the provinces embodied in the existing law."

Mr. Speaker, I think the presentation of a motion such as this is most timely, because today this nation faces a very serious recession. Unemployment is widespread and is a drain not only on our national economy, as such, but on the budgets of the provinces and municipalities. As a

Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations matter of fact I think in a great many respects our nation faces crises in many fields which urgently require examination by both federal and provincial governments.
Members and supporters of the government, in the speeches they have made and through statements contained in the speech from the throne, are claiming that they represent a government which keeps its promises. If there was one promise which recurred throughout the election of last year and the period since, it is that the government was prepared to call another dominion-provincial conference to study the whole question of fiscal relations and consider many of the problems which face the provincial administrations of this country. That promise was clear and definite, and I think the government should announce today that it is being fulfilled.
We in this group have over the years supported the making of grants from the federal treasury to enable the provincial governments to maintain the essential services for which they are responsible. The need for such a policy is evident, because the provincial governments must be in the possession of the necessary financial resources if they are to meet their obligations. Such a claim upon the federal treasury is just, because of the very nature of the federal system.
As hon. members no doubt realize, the head offices of the larger corporations of this country are generally speaking located either in the province of Ontario or in the province of Quebec. Because this is so the profits which accrue to these companies accrue in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, even though their revenue derives from business done in all ten provinces of our nation.
The proposals made in the 1945 green book were very important, far-reaching and imaginative. Since 1945 we have looked to a Liberal government for their fulfilment. Now we look to a Conservative government to make progress in implementing these proposals. The Liberal government which made them was, I think, unnecessarily slow in seeing that they were fulfilled. Even at this date many of the recommendations which were made in 1945 have not been proceeded with.

I wonder if the hon. gentleman would permit a question. Is it not true that the proposals made in 1945 were contingent upon certain action being taken by the provincial governments, which they have never yet been willing to take?
Of course; that is the usual way in which promises were made by the party of which the hon. gentleman is a member-
Respect for the constitution.

There were a number of contingencies, that is perfectly correct. The late Right Hon. Mackenzie King never made a promise in his life if he did not have many avenues of escape to use should he feel at some date that he could not fulfil it, so one would expect in connection with the green book proposals that there would be many avenues of escape available. However, I repeat the statement I have made, namely that in some notable instances important proposals made in the green book of 1945 have yet to be implemented.
Although under our constitution the provinces have very important responsibilities in the field of services we find from experience that under our constitution they have not adequate sources of revenue. As a matter of fact, in the distribution of revenues in this country we find that the federal government receives 70 per cent or more of the tax dollar and that the remaining 30 per cent must be divided amongst all the provinces and the thousands upon thousands of municipalities.
Since the end of the war we find there has been a greater demand on the budgets of municipal and provincial governments than there has been on the budget of the federal government. The budget of the federal government has changed very little since 1945. Expenditures at that time amounted to just over $5 billion, and forecast expenditures today are approximately the same. Generally there has been little or no change in the federal budget compared to 1945. On the other hand the budgets of municipal governments have increased by 246 per cent since 1945, and the budgets of provincial governments have increased by 381 per cent since that date.
The provinces today find it increasingly more difficult to meet the demands that are made on their treasuries, and the municipalities are in a much more difficult position even than are the provinces. It is to make it possible for the provinces to carry on the services that are necessary to the building up of this country, and in turn to make it possible for municipalities to meet their commitments that we are supporting the motion that has been placed before us at this time.
The Prime Minister has made it very clear time and time again that another dominion-provincial conference would be called; and certainly, as has been pointed out, in the face of rising unemployment there is great urgency for the calling of a conference at this time. Surely at such a conference one of the first items on the agenda would be proposals for public works and for national developments

that would take care of the very widespread unemployment that prevails in Canada at this time. If the Prime Minister had reason during the election campaign in 1957 to propose the calling of a federal-provincial conference, there is much more reason for calling such a conference today. Half a million people in this country are unemployed and seeking jobs. Is that not a matter that should be brought before a federal-provincial conference?
The Leader of the Opposition has referred to recent figures for the month of April which indicate that there are 560,000 persons in this country without jobs and seeking work. The figures for unplaced applicants are more recent. Those for May 22 indicate that there are 641,852 unplaced applicants in Canada. This is a drop of just 180,000 from April of this year. This is a smaller drop than occurred last year from April to May in the same statistics when the figure dropped from
545,000	to 360,000; and in the previous year, when the figure dropped from 488,000 in April to 281,000 in May. In other words even with unemployment much more serious today and with the figures of unplaced applicants showing an increase, the absolute rate at which unemployment is dropping is less than it was in either 1956 or 1957. This should be great cause for alarm, because if we were to have unemployment vanish this year we would require to have the rate of unplaced applicants falling much more quickly than it was a year ago.
The situation is critical not only for the people who are unemployed, who lack income and whose families have little means of support, but this problem is serious for the nation as a whole. I have made some calculations concerning the amount of real wealth that has been lost by unemployment in the last year, and my computation indicates that it is between $1,500 million and $2 billion. In other words the serious unemployment prevalent in the nation today affects our real production, our real wealth, the real income of the people of the country, and is having an adverse effect on the revenue of the federal government, the provincial governments and the municipal governments. For this reason it is imperative that action be taken at once and that the government's commitment to call a new federal-provincial conference be carried out.
That the government has committed itself to this is extremely clear. In opening the conference that was held last fall the Prime Minister had this to say:
I would suggest that we might have in mind two days of discussion at this November meeting, first in public and then in committee, after which we
Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations
would adjourn to a later date when we would plan to be ready to consider specific proposals arising out of our first meeting.
It is very clear from this statement that the conference was to be adjourned to a future date. The Minister of Finance, who is in his seat at this time, said on January 29, 1958, in this house as recorded at page 3956 of Hansard:
-an interim measure to take account of the urgency of the present situation and the fact that it was not possible to reconvene the dominion-provincial conference under the pressure of the present protracted session of parliament.
This suggests again that the government intended to call a further conference.
The Prime Minister on November 27 last, as recorded at page 1556 of Hansard, had this to say:
A subsequent meeting as soon as possible in the new year will be held in accordance with the proposals made by this government in calling the conference.
Are you reading from the Prime Minister's letter to Premier Campbell?

No, I am referring to a statement made by the Prime Minister in this house on November 27 last. That statement is a clear indication that another conference would be held early this year. I ask the Minister of Finance why the conference has not been called. I ask the Minister of Finance what is the cause of the delay. I ask the Minister of Finance why the government is not prepared to say at this time that a further conference will be held at an early date.
Certainly the provinces are asking for a conference. It is evident that the municipalities are highly dissatisfied with the treatment they have received. It is not, as the Prime Minister implied the other evening, solely that they are dissatisfied with the treatment they received from the Liberal government. They are also dissatisfied with the treatment accorded them by the present administration.
The submission of the municipal governments to the federal government on February 7 contains the following as found on page A-4:
Since 1945, and increasingly with every passing year, the pressures for urgent and costly programs of local improvements and modern community facilities have continued to mount. There is little prospect that any substantial proportion of these needs can be provided unless facilitating financial assistance can be made available to municipal governments.
There is a clear statement that unless assistance is provided to municipalities to relieve their pressing financial burdens they will not be able to meet the important demands for essential services now being made
736	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations on them. So the municipalities are not satisfied with the results of the one conference that has been held and anything that has been done arising from that conference.
We in this group believe in the principle of federal-provincial tax agreements. We believe that under these agreements the less wealthy provinces should receive substantial payments. We believe the agreements should be used in such a way as to equalize opportunities for citizens all across the nation. We believe that because people live in the have-not provinces so-called or provinces that have a more difficult time financing their administrations they should not have a lower level of public services than people who live in other provinces.
The payment formula today is based in part on the average per capita yield in the two highest provinces. We suggest that this should be changed to bring it up to the highest province. We suggest that there should be consideration of fiscal need and that each province should be paid a stated sum in relation to its population for every dollar per capita personal income falls below the national average. This would mean a substantial measure of equalization in the case of these provinces.
We point out that in a period of recession and falling income such as we are in now provincial revenues are adversely affected. Provincial revenues depend in the main on gasoline taxes, motor licence fees, liquor profits and sales taxes. All of these sources of revenue are tied in very closely with income within the provinces. That being the case, it is most essential that the federal government make it possible for the provinces to stabilize revenues and the income of the people within those provinces.
We believe there should be another factor included in the formula, namely that a prov-vince would not receive in any case less than it received by way of payment the previous year so that the moneys coming from the federal government to the provincial treasury would in each case be assured.
I have said that there are a number of things that could and should be discussed at such a conference. One is the serious unemployment situation facing the nation. The second one I would list is low farm income and the price-cost squeeze affecting the primary producers. At such a conference consideration should be given to whether we are willing to see our agricultural plant deteriorate or whether we are going to adopt policies that will maintain full production of food badly needed throughout the world. The


whole question of the maintenance of farm income should be considered as well as the provision of crop insurance in the various provinces.
The third item we suggest should be considered by such a conference is national development and a national development program that can be shared in by all the provinces. During the last parliament we were very pleased to support loans to the maritime provinces for power development but we think that this good policy of providing money for power development in the mari-times at relatively low rates of interest should be applied to the other provinces. I ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) why the government has not provided this kind of policy for all the provinces and why it has made it applicable only to the maritime provinces. Certainly the province from which I come is asking the federal government at this time for the sum of $100 million by way of a loan for the purpose of power development. I ask him why the policy applied to the maritimes has not been applied equally to other provinces.
At such a conference 1 would suggest that there should be consideration of the development of the roads in our nation. We support the northern development road program outlined in the speech from the throne but I ask the government why a road development program for the people outside the north has not been provided. I suggest that at such a conference the federal government should show its willingness to participate in an expanded road program which would include more than one trans-Canada highway and would include highways running north and south.
The province of Saskatchewan has completed its section of the trans-Canada highway and under the government's normal road development program Saskatchewan will be the only province in Canada that will not be able to obtain any financial assistance this year because its section of the highway has been completed. That province is prepared to enter into an agreement with the federal government for the construction of more highways running east and west and north and south. I ask the Minister of Finance if that is not the kind of road development program we need at this time not only to provide better roads but to help to solve the very serious unemployment problem facing our nation.
We suggest that the fourth item that should be considered at such a conference is the crisis that prevails in our educational system and institutions. I believe most hon. members are acquainted with the fact that Canada has

been very short of graduates in the fields of engineering and medicine in recent years. In spite of our need for more graduates from our universities we find that instead of the situation with respect to entrance fees improving they are going up this year at most universities anywhere from 10 per cent to 25 per cent. Tuition fees are increasing. With unemployment prevailing, it is more difficult for students to obtain the necessary summer employment and we face a real educational crisis.
I suggest that the fifth item that should be considered at such a conference is an overall health program so that the ordinary citizen will not have to pay the very high cost of medical care. A good step is being made in the field of hospitalization at this time. We suggest that it should be extended.
These are some of the things that we suggest must be considered at a federal-provincial conference if the economic crisis facing the nation is to be resolved and a solution of the important problems facing us achieved.
I believe there is another reason why these major issues must be dealt with at this time. We are all aware of the very great advances the Soviet union is making in many of the fields to which I have referred. Canadian businessmen who have recently returned from the Soviet union have said, according to newspaper reports, that at the present rate of increase in production in the Soviet union it is only a matter of time, perhaps 10 or 15 years, until their per capita rate of production exceeds that of the North American continent. We are being challenged across the world today as we have never been challenged before. Is the Minister of Finance going to refuse to call a further federal-provincial conference to deal with unemployment in the face of this great challenge of the Soviet union today?
I suggest to the government that it is not just a matter of comfortable financial arrangements with the provinces enabling them to meet their financial needs. The problem is to make sure that democracy, and our nation, meets the Soviet challenge by increasing our production, by solving our unemployment crisis and by meeting the other important problems to which I have referred.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are some issues that I might have expected the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) to choose as an amendment on such a motion as that now before you. Certainly, however, this would not have been one that I would have expected a sensible Leader of the Opposition to choose as the subject of his amendment today. If there is one subject upon which the people of this country spoke with a clear voice on 57071-3-47

Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations March 31, it was on the subject of the position of this government with respect to the provinces of this country. Apparently there is such a lack of subjects upon which the Leader of the Opposition may choose to found a grievance that he seeks to go back and fight the election all over again on the hustings. If that is what he wishes, there will be no difficulty in gratifying his wish.
I believe the people of this country expected that when the new parliament met the members of this house, in all parties, would be prepared to take account of the fact that the people had spoken decisively on some of these issues. If the Leader of the Opposition wishes to go back and fight these issues over again I can assure him that his wish will be gratified. I believe there are two people in Canada who will not be grateful to him for the speech he has made today.	It does not require very much
guessing as to who those two are. I can think that when the press carries the report of the speech of the hon. gentleman the new Liberal leader in Ontario will not take very much satisfaction out of it. The new Liberal leader in Quebec will not find very much in it to cheer him along his thorny path.
We have heard speeches of this kind before. We heard such speeches during the last session and the session before; yes, on earlier occasions as well. I suppose as long as the Leader of the Opposition and those associated with him lack something new about which to talk we can expect them to go on expressing the same kind of touching concern for Mr. Frost as the Leader of the Opposition undertook to express today. His speech ranged over the issues of not only the 1958 election but the 1957 election as well. I am going to suggest to him that if he hopes to carry his party anywhere from its present position he will have to find something new and fresh about which to talk. The old record, the old story and the old cliches just will not make a very good impression on the Canadian public today any more than they made on the Canadian electorate on March 31.
The Leader of the Opposition appeals on his record. What could have led him to refer to the record of the government of which he was a member? There is no comfort there for him. I can only conclude that it was the pricking of an uneasy conscience that led him today to try to revise and repaint the record of that government of which he was a member. He has endeavoured to give it a fresh coat of paint; anything to give it a new look; anything but the old record in its true colours. We will have an opportunity, I trust, to examine that record, not with the fresh coat of paint that the Leader of

Now, sir, what was the record of the government to which the Leader of the Opposition has himself made reference this afternoon and invited a reference on my part? No one in this house, and few people in this country, are going to forget the attitude of that government toward the provinces year after year. It was not simply a matter of the things they did; it was not simply a matter of the things they left undone; it was their attitude, and that attitude we saw expressed time and again. We saw that attitude expressed in dominion-provincial conference after dominion-provincial conference. It was a haughty attitude, an overbearing attitude. It was a take-it-or-leave-it attitude, a stubborn, stiff-necked attitude. When that government condescended to meet the provinces, they laid the proposals on the table and there was to be no deviation from those. So far as the provinces were concerned, they might take them or they might leave them, but so far as these federal masters were concerned, there would be no change.
As you well know, Mr. Speaker, that attitude was reflected in so many ways. I would have hoped that by this time hon. members opposite would have learned something about the folly of their own attitude. But, sir, only look if you please at the situation in which we found ourselves when we took office last summer. We moved to meet the provinces and the provinces sent their representatives, their premiers, other ministers and officials to meet us here in Ottawa in November.
Five months after the election.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member can count up to five; he has proven that today.
The hon. gentleman can add correctly, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But the hon. gentleman does not seem to be very successful in counting the votes of his party in Canada.
I was able to count a few in my own riding.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, the hon. gentleman is quite unique. I think hon. members ought to grasp the point he is trying to make. He is telling this house, and telling the country, that of the 265 Liberal candidates during the last election, he is unique amongst all the Liberals in being the one Liberal in Canada who increased his majority.
Even that is not true.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It is not the first respect in which we have found my hon.


friend unique. However, Mr. Speaker, I invited you to consider the situation in which we found ourselves. Last fall when we met the provinces, we were determined that there would be no repetition on our part of the attitude of those who had preceded us as representatives of the federal government. We therefore did not face the provinces with any hard and fast, take it or leave it terms. We indicated three measures that, if they approved, we were prepared to take. But we asked them to bring to the conference their proposals. Nothing short of a complete reversal of attitude at that time would have sufficed to break down the wall of suspicion and hostility that had been built up over the years on the part of the representatives of the provinces by those who were then the government, of whom the remnants today sit opposite.
I wonder whether I might ask the hon. gentleman a question?
Ask him two questions.
Does he recall what the premier of Ontario said at that conference about the attitude of the former prime minister in provincial conferences?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. He paid a very generous compliment to Mr. St. Laurent. He reserved his comments in these remarks on those associates of Mr. St. Laurent of whom my hon. friend was one.
I shall read the record shortly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I commend to the hon. gentleman the reading of many records. No one needs it more than he does. With that kind of attitude, we were able to bring about a new atmosphere at that conference. I will say this. A gentleman who has attended many dominion-provincial conferences, and not as the representative of a province with a Conservative government, said to me at the conclusion of the conference that he had attended every conference in the last 25 years but had never seen one the equal of this one for the new spirit, the new attitude that had been created in that conference by the representatives of the federal government.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? Would he mind telling me which member of his delegation he is quoting?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He was not a member of my delegation at all. I have made it quite clear that he was the representative of a province that did not have a Conservative government.

It certainly was not the
premier of British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We put before that conference three things which we indicated we were prepared to do if they met with their approval. In reference to the scheme of hospital insurance we were prepared to remove that veto which the former government had introduced and which would have meant that a minority of the provinces of this country could have prevented the hospital insurance scheme from coming into effect. We indicated that we were prepared, if parliament would support us, to eliminate that provision that required the subscription to the plan by a majority of the provinces representing a majority of the Canadian population. We indicated we were prepared as well to advance the date on which that scheme was to be brought into effect, to remove these crippling fetters on that scheme which hon. gentlemen opposite had imposed.
We then said that we were prepared to remove another limitation on another project that hon. gentlemen opposite had imposed in relation to unemployment assistance. It will be remembered that in the face of our pleas for more generous treatment of the provinces in this matter, when the former government asked parliament to legislate in terms of unemployment assistance it imposed what came to be known as the threshold provision, that there should be no sharing on the part of the federal government with any provincial government in the matter of unemployment assistance costs unless the numbers of unemployed in the particular province exceeded .45 per cent of the population. The hon. gentleman who seconded the amendment today (Mr. Martin) is the hon. gentleman who introduced in this house and defended that threshold provision in order that the federal government would not contribute a cent unless the figures of unemployed exceeded that percentage. We indicated last November to the provinces that we were prepared to eliminate that threshold provision and to contribute dollar for dollar with the provinces to the cost of unemployment assistance.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We indicated we were prepared to move in a third respect, namely in the matter of Atlantic adjustment grants.
I wonder if the hon. gentleman would permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can understand the agitation of my hon. friend when I mention Atlantic adjustment grants.

I should like the minister to tell us if he can, what province, if any, asked to have the threshold removed?
