speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not only had the positions of the various provinces been stated on that point, but our indication of our willingness to make that move was greeted by the provinces then and since. If my hon. friend had done a little bit of touring in the last election campaign he would have heard expressions at that time; I refer to expressions of approval in the provinces by the representatives of the provinces.
That does not answer my question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I went on to speak of our indication of our willingness to take action with respect to Atlantic adjustment grants. Oh, how the Leader of the Opposition talked today about the record of his government! Mr. Speaker, if you will look at the record of that government in reference to Atlantic adjustment grants you just will not find any record. Their achievement in this respect is a zero. This record that he boasts about is a record that could be summed up in one cipher. Not only that, but when we who are on this side of the house today urged consideration of the position of the Atlantic provinces and when those Atlantic provinces themselves at the dominion-provincial conferences prior to the spring of 1956 asked for consideration of the particular position of the Atlantic provinces, they not only got the cold shoulder but a firm refusal on the part of the former government to give any consideration to this question.
You, Mr. Speaker, well know what we did. You well know that we made our statement to the conference last November. That statement was hailed by the provincial representatives. In the official communique that was issued at the conclusion of that conference this sentence took a leading place:
It was generally agreed that the over-all economic position of the Atlantic provinces is now such as to justify some special grants in aid to the governments of those provinces from the federal government.
That is the statement of our position and the statement of general approval on the part of the representatives of the provinces

Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations at that conference. It was in implementation of that general agreement that we proceeded from that point as we did.
The most concrete proposal with respect to the formula for an Atlantic adjustment grant, prior to the 1957 dominion-provincial conference, had been the one put forward at the last previous dominion-provincial conference -indeed I believe at two of them-by the premier of the province of New Brunswick, Hon. Hugh John Flemming. It was in no small degree the vigour of his advocacy of that formula which led to the concrete decisions taken in the fall of 1957. At the conference in November it was agreed that it would be necessary for the Atlantic provinces themselves to decide on their ideas as to what might be a fair basis of division among those four provinces of whatever sum might be made available as an Atlantic adjustment grant. It was for them to decide and those four provinces held a conference of officials at Halifax in December to which the federal government was asked to send representatives to be of whatever assistance they could be in the negotiations. A decision emerged from that Halifax conference to recommend to the governments represented that the Atlantic adjustment grant-whatever it might be -should be divided among those four provinces in the following proportions:	Nova
Scotia 7.5, New Brunswick 7.5, Newfoundland 7.5 and 2.5 for Prince Edward Island, or to give the proportions instead of the amounts that were eventually agreed upon, 3, 3, 3 and 1.
The governments of the Atlantic provinces themselves then made a decision and notified the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) of Canada of that decision. It was their decision. It was a decision by the governments following this conference at Halifax, and Premier Stanfield, having been so notified and authorized by the premiers of the other three Atlantic provinces, advised the Prime Minister of Canada that the four provinces down by the sea were prepared to agree on that formula for the division of the grant.
Then in January of this year we took two steps of very great importance. One of them was indeed of historical importance-it was the Atlantic adjustment grant. For the first time in history recognition was given by the parliament of Canada to the fact that the Atlantic area, embracing the four provinces there, was entitled to a division of revenues from the three joint fields of taxation, on the basis of a special degree of need. It was an historic principle; it was an overdue recognition of a need. We recognized and we advocated it but those who sit opposite and who are prepared to support this amendment

today, not only had not recognized but had indeed vigorously opposed. That is their record on the Atlantic adjustment grant.
We moved to place $100 million at the disposal of these provinces in order to meet that special need and commencing with April 1 of this year there is to be divided among the four Atlantic provinces, in the proportions unanimously agreed upon among them, the sum of $25 million per annum for the next four years.
I think it will be of interest to the people of the Atlantic provinces to read that the Leader of the Opposition came out today and began to talk about the Atlantic adjustment grant. I would have thought that with a modicum of political sense he would know that that is one subject that no Liberal -let alone the Leader of the Opposition himself-would ever wish to hear breathed again.
But we did not stop there. We took into account the fact that it had not been possible to reconvene the dominion-provincial conference-
Why?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Because you were talking too much.
Now at last we have got the real reason.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Can a leopard change his spots? It is a senseless interjection but I suppose it might be misleading to someone who reads the record and did not have the facts, so I will just say in a word that the house was sitting at that time morning, afternoon and night and all day Saturday, and these considerate gentlemen opposite, who had opposed any Atlantic adjustment grant, were saying that we should have another dominion-provincial conference on top of sittings at that pace.
There is going to be full opportunity to discuss these subjects in due course. We then moved to meet the needs of these provinces as urged upon us by the provincial governments because the provinces knew that there was now in office a government which had some recognition and understanding of the problems of these provinces and they did not cease their urgings and their representations in that respect. When the conference rose at the end of November we had additional representations from them and we were urged, particularly by the provincial treasurers who were then in office and were faced in January with the problem of preparing their budgets for submission to their legislatures, for some immediate measure to take care of the current situation. We did move to take care of that immediate situation, and that is how the increase from 10 per cent to 13 per cent in the provincial share of the

personal income tax yield came about as a result of the amendment we introduced in January.
We estimated-and again I emphasize estimate because it depends on the yield from these joint fields of taxation in this fiscal year 1958-59-that this additional sum for distribution among the ten provinces would amount, if the figure for 1958-59 was the same as that for 1957-58, to approximately $62 million. That was just $62 million more than those provinces would have received had there not been a change in government in June 1957.

Would the minister permit a question at this stage; a purely factual question? I take it that payments are being made at this time. Could the minister give us the amount of the instalments paid for the month of April?
Do you want them stopped?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The payments have been duly reckoned in accordance with the provisions of the statute and I can furnish my hon. friend with the figures in due course if he wishes to have them in precise form.
There were two measures taken by us in January of this year. We said that the increase from 10 per cent to 13 per cent was on a one-year basis; it was an interim measure and it was designed to meet the immediate needs of the provinces because they were ready for their budgets. That is the way the matter stood then and that is the way the matter stands today. Those needs have been met in that form for this present.
Now let me straighten out a few things which have been badly cluttered up and which were badly misrepresented in the speech made by the Leader of the Opposition this afternoon. I wish to deal, first of all, with his figures in regard to the federal share of the tax dollar. If, Mr. Speaker, you want figures on the federal share of the tax dollar at the time that tax dollar is collected, I may tell you that the federal share in the fiscal year 1939-40 was 46.5 cents, and if you come down to the 1950's you will find that the figure has varied between 1950 and the last year for which complete figures are available, between 67.7 cents and 72.6 cents of the total Canadian tax dollar.
But if you want to take account of the transfer payments and think just in terms of the revenue finally yielded out of those sources to the provinces and the federal government, here are the figures: in 1939-40 the federal share of the tax dollar after transfer payment was 44 cents; in the fiscal
Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations years 1953-54, 1954-55 and 1955-56, which latter period is the last for which figures are available, it has run between 61 cents and 65 cents.
It is not much use the Leader of the Opposition saying today: well, deduct the cost of national defence. Of course, the cost of national defence has increased compared with 1939, but this is, and always has been, a federal responsibility. Surely it is not germane to this question of what is the revenue of the federal government. We are talking about revenues. There is, of course, the whole question of responsibility. There has been an assumption of some additional responsibility-some responsibilities that go back to the earlier period-but if the hon. gentleman is talking about the federal share of the tax dollar, either in terms of the dollar as collected or of the dollar after the transfer payments among the various levels of government have been effected, the figures are those I have given.
The Leader of the Opposition sought this afternoon to introduce into this debate two issues which I can describe in one word and one word only, "fictitious". He talked about equalization, and he took the opportunity to unburden himself of a charge that those of us who now sit on your right, Mr. Speaker, had voted against the principle of equalization in 1956. He made an equally baseless charge that those of us who were in the house in 1956 had voted against the principle of stabilization. There is not a word of truth in either of these charges. We certainly did vote in 1956 against a measure that was introduced by the former government-the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Agreements Act.
It is true that that measure did embody a provision for equalization and a provision for stabilization, but it embodied some other things too, and we were not prepared to accept those other things. We never voted against the principle of equalization; we never voted against the principle of stabilization. But we did vote against that measure because, as we made perfectly clear at the time that measure was debated, we believed it to be unfair to the provinces and unfair to the municipalities because it did not go far enough. That is all on record, and it is going to take more than speeches such as were made this afternoon by the Leader of the Opposition to change the facts; the facts will, indeed, give little comfort to the hon. gentleman and provide no foundation for the charges he made in this house this afternoon. Those charges are utterly lacking in any basis whatever.
Let me remind the hon. gentleman, in the light of all his talk about the principle of equalization, that in the amendments which

Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations were introduced in January last the principle of equalization was carried further than it has ever been carried before by any action taken by the Canadian parliament.
It was exactly the same principle.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was carried further than it has ever been carried in the history of the Canadian parliament.

Except there was no
stabilization in it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate-
Does that mean that the hon. minister now accepts the principle of equalization on the basis of the position of the two highest provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not what I said at all.
That is what you have never said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We carried the principle of equalization which was written into that act of 1956 and which was supposed to be a crowning glory of Liberal achievement, as it was described here this afternoon, to an extent which hon. members opposite were not prepared to carry it. They can make anything they like out of this talk about equalization but the cap does not fit. The Leader of the Opposition, as the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Montgomery) so rightly said, was simply putting up a straw man. He threshed it, he tore it limb from limb, he pulled its eyes out, set fire to it and then, for good measure, poured acid on it. But it was nothing but a straw man.
Straw men don't have eyes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It was an interesting exhibition, but it had nothing to do with the facts; it was completely divorced from history.
The principle of stabilization continues to be recognized. Had we wanted to interfere with that principle I suppose we would have been expected to propose it last January. But there was no interference with that principle. Every item, every syllable in the principle of stabilization which hon. members opposite invited parliament to place on the statute books is still there; there has been no interference whatsoever, and two provinces, British Columbia and Prince Edward Island, are today deriving from the federal treasury benefits which result from the recognition of the principle of stabilization.

Could I ask the minister a factual question? Is he now asserting that the same principle of stabilization covers the extra 3 per cent of personal income tax that was granted to the provinces in this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker. As the hon. gentleman knows, two sections were added to the act-section 11 and section 12-and one section provides:
-paragraph (f) of subsection 1 of section 2 shall for the purposes of this act and any tax rental agreement, be read and construed as if for the words "ten per cent" therein there were substituted the words "thirteen per cent".
It is perfectly clear.
There is no stabilization there.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Before I leave this subject, let me say just one thing by way of reminding the house of the testimony of the provinces themselves. This is the degree of satisfaction they expressed for the generosity of the treatment they received from the former government, whether on the basis of equalization, stabilization or anything else. The legislation of 1956 contemplated agreements that were to run from April 1, 1957 for a 5-year period. They would have run until March 31, 1962. When we met the provinces, they had all signed the agreement except the province of Quebec; Ontario had signed in respect of one tax instead of three, but the others had all signed for all three.
Did we find they were satisfied with them or, indeed, signed them on the basis of being satisfied with their contents? No, Mr. Speaker, there was not a single province there, regardless of the political colour of its government, which was satisfied with the agreements that had been entered into in pursuance of the legislation passed in 1956 by hon. gentlemen opposite. Not one province. What about Newfoundland, with a Liberal government? What about Prince Edward Island, with a Liberal government? What about Manitoba, with a Liberal government? Were they satisfied? They certainly were not. No provincial governments represented at that conference were more vocal in their denunciation of the inadequacy of the agreement entered into in pursuance of that 1956 legislation than those three provinces represented by Liberal governments. There is the test, surely; the test of the adequacy of the treatment that the provinces received at the hands of the former government.
We did not stop with making provision for meeting fiscal needs on the part of the provinces in the way I have indicated. We went further. We well recall the stony, callous

unwillingness of the former government to enter into measures of partnership with the provinces to carry forward works related to the development of resources. For years we had asked the former government to make some provision for assisting the province of New Brunswick in financing the Beechwood power development but that government would do nothing. All that New Brunswick received was a stony refusal.
On the other hand, we moved, we acted. In a measure that received approval in this house last January we moved to assist the province of New Brunswick with the financing of up to $30 million of the cost of that project which promises to assist so greatly in the development of the resources of the province of New Brunswick. We also moved in the matter of the development of power in the Atlantic provinces and again in legislation that parliament approved at the last session provision was made for federal participation on a partnership basis with the provincial governments in the Atlantic area in the development of power in those areas that will unquestionably be of great assistance in developing the resources of that important part of Canada.
A Liberal measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
And then, looking west, we had not forgotten the way in which that former government or some of its members had talked for years about the South Saskatchewan irrigation dam. South Saskatchewan, what memories that expression conjures up: the discussions in the house, the discussions on the hustings, the former minister of agriculture campaigning up and down Saskatchewan promising the people that if the Liberal government were returned to office they would get their long deferred dam and of course the then prime minister coming along later and saying "No, you will not get it." Well, perhaps talk on that subject served the interests of the former government but talk was all that they ever produced on that subject; we acted.
We have indicated to that province in generous terms the assistance that we are prepared to give to the construction of the South Saskatchewan irrigation dam. If hon. members will look at the supplementary estimates which I had the honour to table in the house this afternoon they will find item 533 under the Department of Agriculture which reads:
Major irrigation and reclamation projects in the western provinces-further amount required, $4,719,600.
Most of that sum is provided for the construction of the South Saskatchewan irrigation dam this year and construction will be
Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations commenced this year if the province of Saskatchewan is prepared now to come forward and enter into the agreement on the very generous terms which we have communicated to its government. Where the former government talked and talked, procrastinated and procrastinated, played politics and shilly-shallied, we have acted.

You still have not got an
agreement.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as hon. members well know this is not the end of the program of the development of resources. The program upon which we were elected to office contemplates that where there are projects that will be of general benefit we are prepared in partnership with the provinces to come forward and assist in those projects. The day of the development of resources in this country is not past. The great day in the development of the resources of Canada lies before us. That was the decision of the people on March 31. And so, far from there being any hidden reason for the actions that we have taken, our actions have been completely open and above board.
I do not pretend for one moment that those actions commend themselves to hon. gentlemen opposite. How could they when they were not prepared to take action along those lines in the long years that they held office here? Again I say there is nothing hidden. The immediate needs of the provinces have been met in the interim measure that was introduced in January and when the time is ripe and there is an opportunity for a resumption of the dominion-provincial conference of course one will be called. There has been no doubt left in the mind of any citizen on that point by the Prime Minister.
This year?
This year, next year, some time, never.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
When the Leader
of the Opposition says that someone does not know our policies then all I can say to him is that if he is not yet aware of our policies at least the people of Canada showed that they are aware of our policies.
As far as unemployment is concerned, we did not wait for any dominion-provincial conference to move to combat the problem and we are not waiting for the provinces today. We took measures that will assist the provinces and municipalities by substantial increases in the fiscal payments to enable them to measure up to their responsibilities in respect of unemployment within their borders. We never at any time waited for a dominion-provincial conference before moving in this field and we are not waiting

Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations today. Our whole program has been designed to discharge fully every vestige of federal responsibility that relates to the unemployment problem. Our responsibilities as a federal government in that respect we will continue to discharge.
We did not wait for any dominion-provincial conference to undertake our vast program of public works. We did not wait for any dominion-provincial conference to weigh the nice question as to what are the relative degrees of responsibility of various levels of government. Again where hon. gentlemen opposite hid their heads in the sand and turned their backs upon their responsibilities, we acted.
The proof of the pudding is in the eating. Compare what has been said here today by the Leader of the Opposition with the attitude of his party when it was in power. The Leader of the Opposition today spoke as though he were the apostle of the provinces, the advocate of the new deal for the provinces. The provinces of this country have not confided to the hon. gentleman the role of advocate and spokesman for the provinces of this country.
Does my hon. friend suggest that he holds that mandate?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The provinces are familiar with the test, "By their fruits ye shall know them." The provinces well know the bitter fruit they were made to eat when my hon. friend was in office and they want no more of that kind of diet. They are not going to ask my hon. friend to be their spokesman and advocate. On the contrary they know that it is this government which in its days in opposition advocated the cause of justice for the provinces. When it had the opportunity this government moved swiftly to meet the needs of the provinces and to discharge to them the responsibilities upon which hon. gentlemen opposite had shamefully turned their backs.

Mr. Speaker, after the vigorous statement we have just heard from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) I think it would be well for us to recall exactly what the precise terms of the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) are so that we can get back to the subject matter which he so ably raised this afternoon. That amendment reads:
That this house regrets that the government has failed to call a federal-provincial conference to discuss unemployment and other urgent problems of common concern to federal and provincial authorities; and that the government has failed to give assurance that it would maintain or improve the principle of equalization of direct tax revenues of the provinces embodied in the existing law.

First of all, in what I have to say by way of comment on the speech of the Minister of Finance I should like to begin with the last portion of the amendment, not that I propose to do what he has done, to seek to divert our attention from the main purpose of the amendment but to indicate the extent to which many of his statements cannot be confirmed or agreed with. The fact is that until very recently it was not possible for any member of the government to say that he was in favour of the principle of equalization. In the last session of parliament during the month of January the Minister of Finance was pressed from all sides of the house to indicate whether or not he was in favour of extending the principle of equalization beyond one year and notwithstanding the pressure imposed on the minister it was not possible to get him to yield one iota from the position he took.
It was the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker), as my leader pointed out, who during the course of the election said in a general statement in Winnipeg, that he was in favour without limitation of the principle of equalization. The statement that we have heard from the Minister of Finance really does not advance us very much. In fact, his statement is to be contrasted with the statement made by the Prime Minister and his declaration likewise is more in harmony with the well known position taken by Premier Frost in the matter of equalization and the position put forward from time to time by the premier of the province of Quebec.
As a matter of fact, the speeches of the Minister of Finance in the house while he was a private member on this subject clearly indicate that he has been in favour of the principle of equalization grants based on need but not, as my leader indicates this party is, on the basis of equalization for all provinces which is quite a different thing. The speeches of the Minister of Finance throughout his career in the house on this particular matter show that he has given emphasis to the question of need and not to the principle of equalization.
I am sorry that the minister had to leave, undoubtedly to attend to more important duties, but I would point out that there could hardly be more important problems before the country at this time than those raised by the amendment put forward by the Leader of the Opposition. We all recognize that the problems of government in this country depend on satisfactory arrangements between the provincial governments and the federal government. It may very well be that hon. members opposite, since we do not hear any more about this tax cut, have recalled the Journals of the House of Commons for Monday, April 1, 1957, when the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), Minister without Portfolio, proposed a motion in these words:
"this house regrets that the economic policy of the government fails, despite a very large surplus, to meet the needs of the Canadian people and in particular . . .
(c) does not assure to the provinces a larger share of the revenues from federal-provincial fields of taxation;-"
This can be found at page 355 of Volume CII of the Journals of the House of Commons for that date. Among those who voted against an assurance to the provinces of a larger share of the revenues from federal-provincial fields of taxation were Messrs. Balcom, Dickey, Fraser (St. John's East), Kirk (Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare), MacEachen, McCulloch

(Pictou), Power (St. John's West), Purdy, Stuart (Charlotte), and Winters, hon. gentlemen whom we do not now have the pleasure of sitting with in this house.
Pleasure!

We in the maritimes are trying to get away from the idea of confederation being a mere affliction which is what the Liberals taught us. The mind of maritime Liberalism as it is revealed in this house has become inconsequential. The only thing it cannot stand is good news. When a factory closes or there is talk of unemployment some Liberal member rises up and flaunts this information.
Rubbish.
They are deliberately trying to erode such progress as we have been able to make since last June.
The voice of the ostrich.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock.

speechtext: Just before I call it six o'clock I would like to suggest to hon. members that perhaps during the dinner hour they read the amendment that is under discussion.

A very good observation.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, before the supper recess, in discussing the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) I had said that some members of the opposition seemed to us to be concerned only with eroding such progress as we have been able to make since last June, especially in the maritime provinces. Consider the vision in fact compared with the vision portrayed in the amendment. It is true that there are now 25 out of 33 members from the four Atlantic provinces on this side of the house but so much remains to be done that we still entertained the hope we could do it together instead of one side trying to make progress and the other side trying to erode.
Consider what remains of the Liberal vision. It consists almost entirely of attempts to deride our vision. The opposition members do have a vision but they never mention it in the house. Their vision is 18 feet, 6 inches across the floor of the House of Commons. It is little wonder that that is

their vision because their new leader tried to get them across into the chosen land without even going through the mechanics of an election. If William Ewart Gladstone were to be dumped among these people they would treat him as one of the non-anointed. They have recently taken up research but it appears now that what they need first is anthropology.
I said at the opening of my remarks, that I would make mention of the third statement by the Leader of the Opposition with which we on this side of the house agree. The Leader of the Opposition said that there Was an "obligation of action". We agree with that. Certainly the members from the maritime provinces agree that there is an "obligation of action". The maritimes have been getting just that since June 10, 1957.

Mr. Speaker, we in this house welcomed most heartily the announcement made the other day by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) when, in referring to the commonwealth conference to be held in the month of September, he said, as found on page 666 of Hansard of Thursday, May 29:
As soon thereafter as it is possible to do so the municipalities of this country are going to be given the opportunity to place their views before the government and before the people of Canada-
We rather regret that he did not set a definite date for the holding of such a meeting. He said that it would be held as soon as possible after the commonwealth conference. However, "as soon as possible" may mean many things to different people and we rather regret that apparently no definite aid will be forthcoming for the municipal governments this year.
I wish to speak on the amendment proposed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) in which he expressed his regret that the government has failed to call a federal-provincial conference and he lists a number of reasons why such a conference should be called. We in this group have long maintained that a new deal with regard to the relationships of the various levels of government with each other is long overdue.
There are two methods of approach. One approach is that of a parallel sharing of responsibilities and a parallel sharing of costs. The other approach was well expounded by the Conservatives while they were in opposition in that they were continuously advocating, not only a realignment of the responsibilities of the various levels of government but also a reassignment of the powers of taxation as they now obtain between the various levels of government.
We in this group have always preferred a new deal that would be based on a parallel
Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations sharing of responsibilities as well as sources of revenue. It is for that and other reasons that the British Columbia section at least of the C.C.F. movement has had over the years as the first item on its program the establishment of a permanent dominion-provincial secretariat. We have these meetings of officials and ministers of the different levels of government going on all the time and we feel that the interests of Canadian unity and harmony would be well served indeed if there were set up, even if need be under the auspices of a minister of the crown, a dominion-provincial secretariat where the various problems and conflicts between the different levels of government could be discussed as they arose.
In addition, we have proposed that there should be not merely temporary agreements between the dominion and the provinces but that an attempt should be made to convene a major constitutional conference in the hope that when we have our 100th anniversary as a nation nine years hence we will have reached agreement as to a new deal for the other levels of government.
For a few minutes I should like to refer to the speech made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) this afternoon. I have long been advised that a successful politician, if he wishes to remain a successful politician, should be able to laugh at himself once in a while, and if I had any advice to give to the Minister of Finance, and this applies equally well to the Prime Minister, I would say that once a week they should look in a mirror and have a good heehaw at themselves.
The Minister of Finance advises us to take account of the fact that the people of Canada have spoken decisively. We are taking account of the fact that the people of Canada have spoken decisively and we realize that almost half the people of Canada have not endorsed those who now occupy the government benches. I should remind the minister that the opposition is usually referred to officially as Her Majesty's loyal opposition and we also have a role to play in the government of Canada. The Conservative party is not the end-all of affairs in Canada.
The minister has made a number of statements in the house of late to which I should like to refer. He has assured us that there is a continuing study of the plight of retired civil servants. He has assured the people of Canada that as far as unemployment is concerned we are past the peak. He has assured the people of Canada that Canadians have a buoyant economy. He assured us in the house not many months ago that at the end of the last fiscal year we would have a balanced budget. He reminds me very much of the politician who did not have the ability to speak without a prepared text and would
754	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations make notes in the margin as to the manner in which he should deliver his argument. He came to a particular spot in his prepared speech and wrote in the margin, "Argument weak here, shout like hell."
I feel that rather than shouting like hell, we in a democracy ought to have a little faith in ourselves and in our ability to resolve the many complicated problems that face us.
I should like to refer to one particular statement of the minister. He said, "we do not impose hard and fast terms". The minister was referring to what he likes to think of as the new kind of deal that they gave to provincial governments. He referred to the Liberals as being like ostriches who hide their heads in the sand. I can think of another animal that works his way into the sand the other way round, and all that you hear is a very beautiful voice shouting like hell and perhaps you see a beautiful face and some very wavy hair. The people have been taken in by that for the time being. However, when the minister says we did not impose hard and fast terms, I should like to remind him of the hard and fast terms that were imposed in relation to the new health insurance plan when the provinces were advised, without negotiation, that mental and tubercular costs could be shared by the federal government only on the condition that they would be deducted from the ordinary grants usually paid to the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not true.
We have been given that understanding and it has not yet been denied. I am pleased to hear the minister now denies it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Read the record without indulging in all that conjecture.

I am very pleased to hear the minister now say that if the federal government now shares mental and tubercular costs under the health insurance plan, that will not be deducted from the grants the province would otherwise receive.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Why do you not
stick to the facts just once?

The minister said that in his opinion sufficient funds were now available to the provincial governments. I am referring to the extra grants which were provided for by this house some months ago. If this was done by negotiation, and if the minister did not impose hard and fast terms upon the provinces, I should like to ask the minister how is it that on a Friday afternoon we in this house were assured British Columbia would receive approximately $5 million more, and on the Monday we were told that was a mistake and British Columbia would receive


only $2 million more. The day following the premier of our province assured the people of his province that they would not get anything more.
I should like to thank my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), for providing me with information as to whether or not this government imposed upon the provincial governments a condition with relation to paying part of mental and tubercular costs under the proposed health insurance plan. I have before me the minutes of the dominion-provincial conference of 1957. I see the following attributed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on page 10:
My colleagues and I have no objection in principle to introducing amendments in parliament to provide for inclusion of mental hospitals and tuberculosis sanitoria, which have been estimated will cost $68 million to begin with if all the provinces come in, and the cost will mount 3'ear by year. But we wish to make clear-
I should like to underline this, Mr. Speaker.
-that whatever is offered to provincial treasuries in this matter cannot be provided in other forms, and in particular must be taken into consideration in any revision of the tax-sharing arrangements act.
The minister branded my statement as untrue. If he wishes to say that his own Prime Minister said something last fall that was untrue, I leave that up to him. The minister says, we did not impose hard and fast terms. Were those terms negotiated with the provinces? Telegrams were supposedly sent to the 10 premiers of the provinces, but I do not know whether or not all of them have ever received copies of these telegrams. We know that at the time the announcement of these terms was made, some of the premiers at least had not even been given the common courtesy of a note informing them what the terms were.
I should like to ask the minister how much negotiation there was with the provinces before the federal government announced they were willing to share in the costs of picnic sites? How much negotiation was there with the provinces before the federal government agreed to pay part of the cost of access roads through our forests? How much negotiation had been conducted with the provinces before there was a change made in the grants payable for hospital construction? How much negotiation went on with the provinces before the federal government announced that the floor had been removed in the sharing of the cost of assistance to the unemployed? No, Mr. Speaker, I am afraid the minister was rather off course when he announced that they did not impose hard and fast terms on the provinces.
I should like further to ask the minister how much negotiation or even consultation

with the provinces there was before this government announced that several hundred million dollars would be expended in the northern areas of Canada, rather than in helping to develop some of the natural resources that are awaiting development in the provinces? The minister calls to witness the reactions of the provincial premiers when he insists that they did not impose hard and fast terms. We are well aware that there are many Conservative provincial premiers who may well have decided, for political reasons, to hide their disappointment. However, the premier of British Columbia certainly cannot be called as a witness in favour of what the federal government has done.
This afternoon the minister made a statement-I do not know whether he was just becoming wildly enthusiastic because of the loudness of his voice-that the immediate needs have been met. I assume he meant the immediate needs of the provinces have been met, and therefore there was no urgency about reconvening the conference.
After many long years this government finally granted to provincial governments increases ranging from 10 per cent to 15 per cent over what they had been getting before. When we consider the needs of the provinces at this time with relation to roads, highways, bridges, education, welfare services and a national health insurance program, is that sufficient? Certainly in so far as the health insurance program is concerned there was no consultation with the provinces because many of the provinces have been asking this federal government to institute a comprehensive national health insurance program rather than the hospital insurance program that his party has presented.
When we consider the needs of the provinces in relation to the development of their resources, I certainly cannot agree for one moment that the immediate needs had been met with the extra grants that were allotted at the last parliament. The situation today, is that all levels of government are faced with a decline in revenues. For the minister that fact may seem to be a relatively unimportant matter because he can resort to the practice of deficit financing. I should again like to underline the dangers involved in that practice.
If the minister is unwilling to impose any measures of economic control and if he is willing to allow inflation to run hogwild, then if he engages in any large scale deficit financing he is going to bring this nation and its economic welfare to the brink of ruin. However, his immediate problem is solved in that he is able to devise ways and means of meeting his bills. However, for our municipalities and our provincial governments there
Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations is no such relatively easy solution. Their income is based on the personal income of the individual citizen and the buying power of those citizens.
Right here I should like to point out one of the weaknesses of even the dominion-provincial tax-sharing agreement, in that so much of the income to the provincial government is based on the level of expenditure or the ability of the individual to spend money. In a time of recession, even the grants payable by the treasury to the provincial governments are subject to very serious reductions indeed. When to that consideration you add the fact that most of the revenues of the provincial governments today are based on the buying power of the average citizen we find the provincial governments in a precarious situation indeed. In our province our 5 per cent sales tax accounts for from one-quarter to one-third of the revenues of our government. If people are unable to buy other than the bare necessities of life the revenues of our government are going to decline; and they have already declined very seriously indeed. If this government wanted to do anything really worth while for the provinces they might consider the possibilities of underwriting the level of expenditures that are now found necessary in the provincial field.
The agreements between the federal government and the provincial governments used to be founded on certain basic principles. We may have had our arguments with regard to some of them. However, at the present time I am becoming convinced that they are now based on political expediency pure and simple. The procedure is like that of a good many men I used to watch in my younger days when they used to deal in horses. It is some political horse trading. That seems to be about all that I can find by way of principle in the methods now adopted.
We used to have the principle of equalization of the wealth of the nation. When I lived in Saskatchewan years ago, I well remember the argument put forward with regard to so much of the insurance money we paid, the money we paid for the farm implements we had to buy and in respect of many of our other major expenditures. It was contended that the money went to the province of Ontario and that as that was the place where these corporations paid their taxes, it was therefore only right that there be such a thing as an equalization principle and that some of that money be returned to the government of our province. The province of Ontario and the province of Quebec have never liked the equalization principle. The outstanding spokesman in the Conservative party in this house over the years against

Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations the equalization principle has been the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer). I certainly hope that before this debate is concluded we shall see the hon. member for Three Rivers taking his part in it in order that we may hear what the Duplessis government now has to say on this whole subject of dominion-provincial financial arrangements.
There was a retreat from the principle of equalization with the introduction of the stabilization factor. The richer provinces put up such a howl that we were obliged to introduce what we call the stabilization factor so that the richer provinces who paid the lion's share of taxation would not suffer unduly. Equalization was retained to some extent in order that there might be some money over and above the normal amount for the have-not provinces. I always regretted this factor entering the scene, but it is now part of the pattern.
We in our group contend that a third consideration must now enter the picture, namely the need for national development.
I am all in favour of the spending of a great deal of money, if need be, in northern Canada. While some argument may be found for building a railway from igloo 'to igloo and a highway from Eskimo hut to Eskimo hut, at the same time it must be remembered that we have vast resources in the provinces of Canada in which most of the people of Canada live. The development of these resources is a matter which is beyond the abilities of the provincial governments. We feel that the time is long past when the federal government should begin to assume some responsibility.
Reference has been made to the rather generous-at least in the eyes of the government-terms that have been given to the Atlantic provinces. We are all in favour of them. If my reading of the proceedings of meetings of the federal authorities and the provincial premiers is correct, I believe it was the premier of British Columbia and the premier of Saskatchewan who were most insistent that something be done to restore the economic life and welfare of the people of the Atlantic provinces. What we do not like to see-and I am sure the premier of British Columbia and the premier of Saskatchewan do not like to see it-is the fact that these sums of money are now paid as a handout. I know that is typical Conservative philosophy; charity for the poor but a fair deal never.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What drivel!

They insist upon taking whatever is in their power to take. Then they exercise charity to those who have been a [Mr. Regier.l

little less greedy than they have been along life's way. I am sure that the people of the Atlantic provinces would like to know that they are citizens of Canada, that they have a right to the wealth of the Canadian nation and that they do not have to receive handouts at the hands of this federal Conservative government.
When we plead for more money, we realize that this federal government must retain fiscal and monetary control within the nation. We are not centralists. However, we hope we are realists.
We do not wish to rob the central government of that. We do not like, however, the other levels of government-and I never call them the lower levels-to be treated as poor relations.
I would like to close my remarks by again expressing my pleasure at the announcement that some time after September there will be an unofficial dominion-municipal conference. We believe in the parallel sharing of responsibilities and revenues by the various levels of government. We have called for the establishment of a permanent dominion-provincial secretariat in the interests of national unity to prevent these conflicts from arising as they have arisen in the past. We appeal for a constitutional conference of major significance and scope.
We do not agree with the minister that this government did not impose its will. We believe it imposed its will in a harsher manner than any other government has done, and they did it, in our opinion, for one purpose only-to win the last election. We believe that the present plight of our provincial and municipal governments is serious indeed and that in any new arrangements we should maintain the principle of equalization-stabilization if you will-but also with an eye to national development within the provinces. We feel there is no way out in the light of the current situation, with revenues declining for all governments, except to adopt the C.C.F. program of a planned economy in order to be able to implement these recommendations.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. J. Browne (Minisier without Portfolio):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the speech of the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) this afternoon, but I must say his speech was very puzzling to me. I have in my hand his amendment which falls into two parts, two principal parts at any rate. The first dealt with his criticism that the government had failed to call a federal-provincial conference to discuss unemployment and other urgent problems of common concern and the second part with his criticism that the government had failed

to give assurance that it would maintain or improve the principle of equalization of the direct tax revenues of the provinces embodied in the existing law.
With respect to the first part he said nothing; I do not recall one statement by the Leader of the Opposition in regard to the first part of his motion. He dealt with the second part but the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) dealt with the first part when he gave us a brief resume of some of the arguments he advanced in the debate which took place in this house a few days ago. I think I should at least thank him for his acknowledgment that full responsibility does not rest on the present government for unemployment conditions in Canada and I wish he would preach that point to other members of his party, some of whom seem to think that it does. I think the hon. member should also remind them of the contents of the document furnished to members of the previous government on March 31 of last year when they were certainly warned as to what was going to happen in regard to unemployment in this country.
Most people throughout the country in the recent election, I believe, held the same view -that full responsibility did not rest upon the present government. In fact, the people of Canada recognized that no responsibility for the existing unemployment conditions fell on the shoulders of this government. I believe that hon. members on the other side of the house, if they are fair, will recognize that the unemployment situation in Canada is not just a condition peculiar to this country because trade is a two-way affair and if we cannot sell our goods it means that somebody else cannot buy them. The best customer we have, of course, is the United States, and it means that they are not buying as much and that they are not selling as much, either. Actually they have a tremendous unemployment problem in the United States and anyone who has followed the activities of the government there in trying to solve the problem will see they have done some of the things we have done, although I would submit that they have not done nearly as much and they have not been quite as effective in this respect as we have been.
Some of the previous speakers on the other side of the house referred to some of the things we have done and I would like to remind the house of the large number of things we have done to help reduce unemployment in this country, which have indeed eased that situation. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has already referred to the action of the federal government in assuming the full cost of half the unemployment expenditures in the provinces. Half the total
2. 1958	757
Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations cost of social assistance is now being borne by this government; we increased the old age pensions and it is well known that many people who, perhaps, had not many of this world's goods, have been able to benefit by the increase in the old age pension. Similarly, we have increased old age assistance and the blind pensions and pensions for the disabled. We increased unemployment insurance seasonal benefits and I believe many people are inclined to forget that we actually increased the amount payable in respect of those benefits, in addition to extending them last year by six weeks. We gave more benefits; we increased the ratio from 50 per cent to five-sixths. In other words, a person who had we will say 20 stamps would, under the previous administration, get ten weeks' unemployment insurance seasonal benefits. Under our arrangement he would get about 17 weeks' or 70 per cent more unemployment insurance benefits than he did under the previous government. This season we have also extended by six weeks unemployment insurance seasonal benefits.
We started a big housing program last year when parliament voted over $300 million, resulting in greater housing construction than had ever been undertaken in this country. The number of houses which were being built last winter was the greatest number on record, and there is nothing which responds so well to artificial assistance as house construction. In this way it is estimated that
200,000	more people were employed as a result of the stimuli given than would otherwise have been employed.
We made money easier and that had >
the effect of putting more funds into circulation and in turn enabling more houses to be built and other activities undertaken, thus creating additional employment. We made arrangements with the provinces by which access roads to natural resources and access roads with a tourist value could be built on a 50-50 basis and we also arranged with the provinces to go 50-50 on the construction of such things as picnic grounds, camp sites and that sort of thing. I will admit that this is not a very great development, but I know from experience in my own constituency that it has meant here and there that a considerable number of people did get employment and useful work was undertaken.
Then, as was mentioned by the previous speaker, the increase in the allowance for hospital construction by doubling the grant has been of great assistance to the provinces in helping them in their hospital programs. Moreover, bringing in this hospital program on July 1 will enable Newfoundland and, I think, some other provinces to begin to get the benefit of the expenditure by the federal
753	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations government on July 1 instead of having to wait until next year. That is going to be a tremendous thing as far as Newfoundland is concerned, and I think it will amount to between $4 and $5 million a year benefit to Newfoundland.
Turning now to public works, I heard the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) challenge hon. members on this side of the house to say what public works-he qualified his question by adding "of a national character"-have been undertaken. He was referring to some major undertakings. Well, he knows as well as I do that no great public work of a major character has been inaugurated since this house opened, nor could it have happened before this house opened.

If the hon. gentleman would permit me, the question I asked was: can he name a project which this government initiated and which has actually been started and, if it has been started, how many men have been put to work as a result.

I admit the validity of that question, and I cannot personally point to anything that has actually given great employment, but I do know of a number of works for which money will be voted in the estimates or in the supplementary estimates. The Minister of Finance has drawn attention to the vote of $4 million in the supplementary estimates tabled today for the South Saskatchewan river dam.
That is for all the year.

Maybe, but you cannot start a $100 million program within a few minutes-I think the hon. member will realize that. We have a project for harbour development in St. John's, Newfoundland, with which hon. members in the Liberal party opposite are familiar. That has been under consideration for several years; it was under consideration by the Liberal government, but they did nothing about it.

Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Is he not aware that the planning of this project was started by the previous government and carried on continuously by the present government, and that there was no change at any time?
I am perfectly familiar with the investigation that was conducted.
And that is all that is going on now?
Oh no, there is more going on now.

All you did was talk
about it.
Perhaps the hon. gentleman would permit a second question?

Let me
answer this question first. This project was planned under the auspices of the previous government but the plans were put on the shelf.
I do not think they even got to the shelf.
They were being worked on on the drawing boards.
They did not even get off the floor, let alone up to the shelf.
Would the hon. gentleman mind answering my second question now? Would he tell me how many people are now employed on the harbour at St. John's? There are none.

I cannot give you that figure, but I have no doubt the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) will be pleased to supply the information. I am trying to indicate the number of methods by which this government is trying to ease the unemployment situation and increase the number of people employed.
We gave assistance to the coal mining industry by increasing the subsidy to that industry in the maritime provinces and in Alberta. And it must always be remembered that according to the figures given by the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin) there were more people working this year on April 15 than there were last year at the same time.
Then again, we gave assistance to the maritime provinces in the construction of thermal power plants, and I believe something in the neighbourhood of $10-12 million will be spent on these projects this year.
Another very important effort on the part of this government to assist provinces to provide employment for the people who reside there-and it must be remembered that it is not entirely a federal problem; the provinces have their share in regard to the solution, too-is by the special maritime adjustment grant of $25 million. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate knows that the province of Newfoundland will receive $7,500,000 out of that $25 million, in addition to $1,600,000 from the increase of 3 per cent of the income tax, and as a result of that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate happens to be the only one who increased his vote in the last election.

On a question of privilege, I do not like to be given that honour. Every Liberal member in Newfoundland increased

his vote, and, to be fair, I must admit that the Conservatives did, too.

Every Liberal member may have increased his vote, but he did not increase his majority. I am not sure the hon. member did this.
This house has not yet been told of the very interesting campaign we had in Newfoundland. We had some distinguished visitors from the mainland, including the Leader of the Opposition, and he could tell a tale if he wished about his experiences. However, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is aware that on the strength of the assistance that the federal government gave in supplying the $7,500,000 and the $1,600,000 to the Liberal government in the province of Newfoundland, the premier of Newfoundland announced publicly that he was embarking on a program of spending over $100 million. I will give the house details, and show how this was to be made up. He was going to spend $56 million on building roads, $20 million on building schools, $20 million on hospitals and $5 million on rural electrification.
Over what period?
I presume it is over a three-year period.
Longer than that.
Yes, it will take you much longer than that.
You have hit the nail on the head.
That is what the premier said.

Before that plan was announced the government of Newfoundland did not have a cent to spend on anything. They had adjourned the house; the assembly was adjourned, and the premier was waiting to hear what he was going to get from Ottawa from this adjustment grant. It was presumably on the strength of what he knew he would get that he was enabled to announce this $100 million expenditure.
I see today in the newspaper a statement of the minister of highways in Newfoundland that of the 600 miles of road he is going to pave in three years under an accelerated program, 100 miles will be done this year, 200 miles next year and 300 miles the year after. Our people are accustomed to pie in the sky; we are accustomed to a lot of promises being made in advance, as the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate knows as well as anybody, and perhaps better than anybody. So we only have 100 miles to be paved this year. But, as hon. members concerned with this province will know, the cost of paving there is extremely high and to pave

Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations 100 miles of highway would cost in the neighbourhood of $10 million. Perhaps the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate could tell me if I have underestimated the cost of it.
I do not pretend to be an expert.

I will look at the list and see if there is something here for the hon. member. There is reference to a road from Gander to Gambo, a distance of eight miles. I believe that is in the hon. member's district.
Three miles of that would be in my district.
There is also reference to the veterans' housing road, Gander, a distance of two and a half miles but I do not think that is in the hon. member's district.
No.

I will resist the temptation of dwelling on this at length. Although it is interesting I will not embark on a further discussion of this matter.
There was, of course, other assistance given to the provinces through increasing the formula on personal income tax from 10 per cent to 13 per cent. As far as Newfoundland is concerned it received $9 million which has made possible this expenditure to which I have referred. If it is possible in Newfoundland then similar expenditures are possible in the other Atlantic provinces, namely New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia.

In 1939 we had the second world war, and afterwards we had industrial expansion, a raise in the standard of living of the Canadian people and the gradual development of social security; there was also the Korean war, the cold war, the scientific revolution of war machines and the conquest of space by Russia which is a challenge to the western countries and a formidable threat to world peace. Dominion-Provincial Fiscal Relations
Our opponents from Quebec were also shocked by the fact that the federal government entered the field of direct taxation. They contended that the federal government was violating an exclusive right of the provinces, forgetting that in 1917 the Conservative federal government imposed a direct tax without anybody accusing them of violating the provincial rights.
In 1942, in order to provide for the increasing expenditures which already were $3,742 million, an agreement was signed between the federal government and the provinces, whereby the provinces rented the field of direct taxation for a five year period. In 1946, at the end of the first federal provincial agreement, the national expenditures were still $2,850 million.
Therefore, the fiscal problem had not been solved. Consequently, the federal government asked for a renewal of the agreement for an additional period, in order to find a solution which would allow the provinces as well as the federal government to provide for new financial needs, without imposing double taxation.
Notwithstanding the many statements of the premier of the province of Quebec to the effect that the provinces had an exclusive or a priority right in the field of direct taxation, everyone recognizes that the federal government and the provinces have an equal and concurrent right to it, and there was never any question, on the part of the federal government, of violating any of the provincial taxation rights, as has been contended for so long by the supporters of the Union Nationale. In any event, the premier of Quebec refused-for reasons which I then believed, and believe even more today, to have been of a political nature-to sign the agreements for a definite period, thus causing the people of Quebec to lose the millions of dollars to which our province was entitled.
During the federal-provincial conferences where the serious fiscal problem was being discussed, the Quebec premier never made any concrete suggestion or proposal to solve this thorny problem. He merely indulged in generalities and demagogic platitudes.
After much study and effort, the Liberal government developed the 1955 solution which permitted, among other things, either the rental of direct taxation rights or the 10 per cent deduction from direct taxation. That solution also provided the imaginative and fair method of paying a subsidy which,


on a per capita basis, would allow each province to receive its fair share of the national revenue without double taxation.
But here too, our opponents came out against the principle of equalization, declaring it unacceptable. Not until June 10, and the increase of deductibility of 3 per cent did our opponents seem to want to take credit for introducing equalization, and now they also state that this deduction is a safeguard for the provincial rights of Quebec.
And what about the attitude of the Union Nationale party with regard to federal subsidies? It is clear, from the history of our country, that the fathers of confederation and those who fought most zealously to protect provincial autonomy never considered federal subsidies as being incompatible with autonomy, because at the time of the interprovincial conference of 1887, the constitution was amended so as to allow for an increase of federal subsidies to the provinces, and subsequently, from time to time, the latter asked the federal government for a further raise of these annual contributions.
Only in the province of Quebec, and in comparatively recent times, was an already complex problem wilfully made more so on the claim, inspired by political reasons, that the acceptance of federal subsidies of any kind was the complete negation of provincial autonomy. And yet each year the Quebec government receives $27,323,000 in subsidies from the federal government. This latter figure is for the financial year ending on March 31, 1957. Of those subsidies, there are the statutary ones coming from the special corporation tax, the technical school subsidies which actually come within the field of education; subsidies for the building of hospitals, for public health, for the control of tuberculosis and cancer, for mental health, for old age pensions, for pensions to the blind, for the disabled and for other things.
Those subsidies, Mr. Speaker, are administered exclusively by provincial governments and in the province of Quebec it was even found possible to work out patronage and discrimination with some of those federal subsidies.
